raw:
Morning light lies pale across the library tables. Professor Stone is at the desk beneath the spiral stair, sorting returned books into a cart.

When you ask about the human seat’s last active years, and whether original records are available, he sets aside his blue pencil.

“The public record is uneven, but it exists.” He draws out several volumes. “Start with the *Council Proceedings* for the final sessions with a seated human delegation. They preserve speeches, votes, and adopted resolutions—edited, of course.”

He adds a thinner register. “This tracks committee referrals and appointments. Less readable, more useful if you want to know what happened to a proposal after it left the chamber.”

A third set of booklets follows: *Annual Reports of the Human Delegation*. “Budgets, petitions received, travel, staff appointments. They become sparse near the end.”

You ask after originals. Stone’s hand rests briefly on the top booklet.

“Not open to students. The original minute books, correspondence, and private memoranda are restricted Covenant history. Chancellor Ashworth’s signature is required.” He nods toward the locked cabinet along the far wall. “These are contemporary printed records, not later summaries. They’re the closest open starting point.”

He carries the stack to a reading table beneath a lamp and sets the committee register on top.

“If you identify a specific record you need, bring the request to me before you take it to the Chancellor.”

The library settles around you again: lamp oil, paper, the faint turn of pages from the upper gallery. Before you lie the public record of a seat that went vacant sixty years ago.
